criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly identifies the majority-class floor and the ~92% accuracy trap under 8% prevalence, names appropriate imbalance-aware metrics (ROC-AUC/PR-AUC/F1), proposes a valid simple-model baseline, and states correct comparison-validity conditions (shared split, leak-free preprocessing, same metric). Deduct for factual errors such as claiming 93% accuracy is strong, misstating what a trivial model scores on ROC-AUC/PR-AUC, or proposing an invalid comparison setup.

Full marks: covers the full ladder — trivial/naive baseline, simple-model baseline, and incumbent/heuristic baseline — plus interpretation-as-lift and at least one diagnostic or variance/uncertainty consideration. Deduct for each missing tier or for omitting the interpretation-as-lift and validity discussion.

Full marks: justifies WHY each baseline exists (floor, reasonable-effort reference, business benchmark), reasons explicitly that 0.82 is only meaningful as lift, and argues the decision consequence (e.g., prefer the simpler model when the gap is small). Deduct when baselines are listed without rationale or when no decision is drawn from the comparison.

Full marks: organized (e.g., an ordered ladder with concise justifications) and readable at design-review altitude, using correct vocabulary. Deduct for disorganized, rambling, or ambiguous explanation that a reviewer could not act on.

expected_answer_points: Establish a trivial/naive floor first — a majority-class predictor (and/or base-rate / stratified-random guess) — to define the absolute lower bound before any learned model

Recognize the imbalance trap: with 8% positives the majority classifier already achieves ~92% accuracy, so '93% accuracy' is near-worthless and accuracy is the wrong metric; prefer ROC-AUC and especially PR-AUC / F1 / recall-at-precision for the rare class
Add a simple, low-tuning model baseline (regularized logistic regression or shallow tree with basic preprocessing) as the 'reasonable-effort' reference the complex model must beat
Include an incumbent/heuristic or human baseline (the current churn rule or process) because lift over it is what justifies the project to the business
Interpret 0.82 as lift over the baselines rather than in absolute terms — a small gap over logistic regression means the added XGBoost complexity is not justified and the simpler model should win
Use baselines as diagnostics for target leakage or a broken split (trivial baseline scoring too high, or the complex model looking implausibly good)

State the validity conditions: identical CV split/folds, identical preprocessing fit on training data only, same metric, fixed seed, and report variance/confidence (CV std or bootstrap) so lift is judged against noise
common_pitfalls: Accepts or defends the 93% accuracy as good, missing that a majority-class predictor already reaches ~92% under 8% prevalence
Treats a tuned logistic regression or 'another ML model' as the only baseline and skips the trivial majority-class / base-rate floor entirely
Judges ROC-AUC 0.82 as 'good' in absolute terms instead of as lift over the baselines, so never asks whether XGBoost's complexity is justified over a simple model
Compares models evaluated on different splits, metrics, or with preprocessing fit on the full dataset (leakage), invalidating the comparison
Omits the incumbent/heuristic or human baseline that the business actually needs the model to beat
Ignores the diagnostic role of baselines (catching target leakage or a broken split) and reports no variance/confidence, treating a single fold's number as definitive
reference_answer:
Before trusting any single number I'd insist on a ladder of baselines, each evaluated on the identical CV split, preprocessing, and metric as the XGBoost model.

1. Trivial / naive baseline: a majority-class (always-predict 'no churn') predictor, plus a base-rate or stratified-random guesser. This sets the absolute floor. Crucially, on an 8% positive rate the majority classifier already scores ~92% accuracy, so the teammate's '93% accuracy' is almost meaningless — it barely beats predicting nothing. This exposes accuracy as the wrong headline metric under imbalance; I'd switch the conversation to ROC-AUC and, given the rarity of the positive class, PR-AUC / F1 or recall at a fixed precision, since a trivial model gets ROC-AUC ~0.5 and near-zero PR-AUC.

2. Simple-model baseline: a regularized logistic regression (with basic one-hot encoding + scaling) or a shallow tree. This is the 'reasonable-effort' reference the complex model must beat to justify its cost and opacity.

3. Incumbent / heuristic baseline: whatever rule or human process currently flags churn today. Lift over this is what actually justifies the project to the business.

Interpretation: 0.82 is meaningful only as lift, not in isolation. A large gap over the trivial baseline plus a clear gap over logistic regression confirms real signal and that the extra model complexity is earning its keep; if XGBoost barely beats logistic regression, ship the simpler, more maintainable model. Baselines are also diagnostics: if a trivial baseline scores surprisingly high, or XGBoost looks implausibly good, suspect target leakage or a broken split.

Validity conditions: every model must share the same train/validation folds (or CV scheme), the same preprocessing fit only on training folds, the same metric, and a fixed seed. I'd also report cross-validation variance (or bootstrap CIs) so the lift is judged against noise, not a single lucky fold.
